nameStory: The 'horned' in this spider's name comes from small projections or bumps on its abdomen that give it a somewhat spiky appearance. As a 'parasitic' cobweaver, it earned its name by living in or near the webs of larger spiders, sometimes stealing prey or scavenging rather than building its own substantial web.
description: The Horned Parasitic Cobweaver is a tiny member of the comb-footed spider family, measuring only a few millimeters across. These diminutive spiders have small, rounded abdomens with distinctive bumps or projections that give them their 'horned' appearance. They're part of the cobweb spider group, known for their irregular, tangled webs made of sticky silk. You'll need to look closely to spot these minuscule arachnids, as they're among the smaller spiders you'll encounter in New England.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small spider, typically just 2-3mm in body length - about the size of a small ant or grain of rice

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small bumps or horn-like projections on the rounded abdomen create a slightly spiky texture when viewed up close

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small, irregular cobwebs or may be found in association with larger spiders' webs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found near or within other spiders' webs, exhibiting kleptoparasitic behavior by stealing prey

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brown or tan coloration that helps it blend in with web debris and dead insects

habitat: Found in various habitats throughout New England where other spiders are active, including gardens, forest edges, and around human structures. They particularly favor areas with abundant spider webs from larger species, as they often live as kleptoparasites. Look for them in shrubs, low vegetation, and corners of buildings where multiple spider species congregate.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to establish territories near other spiders' webs. Mating activity increases during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and females are producing egg sacs containing about 42 tiny eggs each. Best time for observation and identification.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active into early fall, though numbers may decline. Late-season egg laying occurs before winter approaches.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as juveniles or in egg sacs protected in sheltered locations.

funFact: Despite weighing only about 11 milligrams (less than a grain of sugar), female Horned Parasitic Cobweavers can produce egg sacs containing over 40 eggs, each one carefully crafted to be perfectly spherical and measuring less than a millimeter across!
confusionNotes: Often overlooked entirely due to their tiny size, or mistaken for debris in spider webs. The key difference from other tiny spiders is the distinctive bumpy or horned texture of the abdomen - run a magnifying glass over what looks like web debris and you might spot one moving!
contextualKnowledge: The term 'parasitic' in this spider's name doesn't mean they're parasites in the traditional sense - they don't live on or inside other animals. Instead, they're 'kleptoparasites,' meaning they steal food from other spiders' webs rather than always catching their own prey.
compareHints: As the only Neospintharus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other tiny comb-footed spiders in the Theridiidae family. Unlike most of its relatives, the Horned Parasitic Cobweaver has those distinctive abdominal projections and shows more kleptoparasitic behavior. Other small theridiids typically build their own complete webs rather than associating with other spiders' webs.
